THE COURSE / YOUR ROADMAP
SMALL STEPS. SOLID FOUNDATIONS.
A language. A toolkit.
A database of your own.
Learn how things work by building them from the ground up.
ALGORITHMS / BIG O
More data. How much more work?
Big O describes an asymptotic upper bound on growth. Compare these simplified growth curves, then connect them to the algorithms you write.
2 items1,024 items
Illustrative units, not timings or exact operation counts. Constants, hardware, and implementation affect actual runtime.
Logarithmic bar scale · every grid interval is ×10
Time and space
Measure how work grows and how extra memory grows. Iterative binary search uses O(log n) time and O(1) extra space.
State the case
Insertion sort is O(n²) in the worst case, O(n) for already sorted input, and O(1) in extra space.
State the assumption
Binary search needs sorted data. A hash table can offer O(1) average lookup, while its worst case can be O(n).
What comes after the prototype?
The full syllabus will add strings and recursion, multi-file programs, debugging and undefined behavior, linked lists, hash tables, trees and graphs, binary storage, B+ tree indexes, and transaction recovery. These are planned lessons; the eight exercises above are available now.


THE CAPSTONE / TINYDB
BUILD YOUR UNDERSTANDING INTO SOMETHING REAL
Your own database.
One small piece at a time.
Turn pointers, structs, and algorithms into a system you understand.

↓
ROW STORAGE{ id: 1, name: "Ada" }
The build plan
01
Represent a row AVAILABLE
Give each record an ID and a name using structs.
02
Insert & query AVAILABLE
Build a command loop and find rows with a table scan.
03
Store it on disk PLANNED
Serialize rows into pages and persist them in browser storage.
04
Make queries fast PLANNED
Replace a full scan with a B+ tree index.
05
Recover safely PLANNED
Add a write-ahead log and simulate interrupted writes.
Small on purpose
TinyDB currently uses an in-memory table and simple insert/select commands. It resets between runs. SQL, disk persistence, indexes, and transactions are future milestones.

UNDER THE HOOD
A real browser C lab.
Clang and LLD are compiled to WebAssembly. Your source compiles and runs locally in a Web Worker. No compilation server is involved.
This prototype uses the experimental wasm-clang toolchain. It supports C17 and a subset of WASI. Native processes, sockets, and some system APIs are unavailable. Programs have a 5-second execution limit; standard input is provided before running.
Source, input, and completed lessons are saved in this browser. Program files and database rows are temporary. Output checks are practice aids, not a security-grade assessment.
